about: LAWS0002 is UCL Laws' compulsory 30-credit first-year property module, taught in person across Terms 1 and 2 and assessed in 2026/27 by a 100% examination. It introduces what makes a right proprietary rather than personal, how property rights are created and transferred, and how competing claims are prioritised, with a detailed focus on land law and close reading of statute and case law. UCL does not publish an ordered topic list, and the 2026/27 catalogue entry does not name individual topics such as leases, easements or mortgages, so this pack's topics are built from the official description and the core areas of English land law; check your module reading list for exactly which topics are examined. Trusts in general are taught in Property II in Year 2.

notes.h: Property rights, personal rights and the 1925 framework
notes.body:
Property law asks what makes a right "proprietary" rather than "personal", and why that matters. The answer shapes the whole of land law.

Why the distinction matters
- A personal right (for example, a contractual right or a licence) binds only the person who granted it.
- A proprietary right is a right in the land itself. It is capable of binding third parties, such as a purchaser or a mortgage lender, and survives the grantor's insolvency.
- Most land law disputes are therefore about priority: when two people claim rights in the same land, whose right wins?

Which rights are proprietary?
English law recognises a limited list of property rights (sometimes called the numerus clausus principle), and the courts are reluctant to add to it.
- National Provincial Bank v Ainsworth [1965] AC 1175: a deserted wife's "equity" to stay in the matrimonial home did not bind the bank that lent to her husband. Lord Wilberforce said that, before a right can be admitted into the category of property, it must be definable, identifiable by third parties, capable in its nature of assumption by third parties, and have some degree of permanence or stability. Parliament responded by creating statutory home rights (now in the Family Law Act 1996).
- Hill v Tupper (1863) 2 H & C 121: an exclusive right to put pleasure boats on a canal was only a personal licence, not an easement.
- Licences are personal. A contractual licence did not bind a purchaser in King v David Allen [1916] 2 AC 54, and in Ashburn Anstalt v Arnold [1989] Ch 1 the Court of Appeal said a contractual licence does not create an interest in land, although a constructive trust may bind a purchaser whose conscience is affected.

The 1925 legislation
The Law of Property Act 1925 (LPA) simplified the system:
- Only two legal estates can exist: the fee simple absolute in possession (freehold) and the term of years absolute (leasehold) (s1(1)).
- Legal interests are limited to those in s1(2), the most important being easements for a term equivalent to a legal estate and charges by way of legal mortgage.
- Every other estate or interest takes effect in equity (s1(3)): for example, interests under a trust, restrictive covenants, estate contracts and life interests.

Legal and equitable rights
Legal rights are created by following the formalities (usually a deed and, for registered land, registration). Equitable rights can arise more informally, for instance where there is a specifically enforceable contract (Walsh v Lonsdale (1882)). Historically, legal rights bound everyone, while equitable rights bound everyone except a bona fide purchaser of a legal estate for value without notice. Today, the registration systems largely replace the doctrine of notice.

What is "land"?
Land includes buildings and other things attached to it (LPA s205(1)(ix)). Whether an object is a fixture (part of the land) or a chattel depends on the degree and purpose of annexation. In Elitestone v Morris [1997] 1 WLR 687, a bungalow resting on concrete pillars was part of the land because it could not be removed without being destroyed.

Two systems
- Registered land (Land Registration Act 2002): title is recorded on a central register. Most titles in England and Wales are now registered.
- Unregistered land: title is proved by deeds, and priority depends on the Land Charges Act 1972 and, for residual interests, the doctrine of notice.

Exam tips: When analysing any right, ask: is it capable of being proprietary? Is it legal or equitable? Has it been created with the right formalities? Is it protected so that it binds the person now claiming the land?

notes.h: Creating and transferring interests: formalities and proprietary estoppel
notes.body:
Land law insists on formalities because land is valuable, transactions are complex and third parties need to be able to discover rights. A typical sale has three stages: contract, completion (transfer by deed) and registration.

Stage 1: the contract
Section 2 of the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989 provides that a contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land can only be made in writing, incorporating all the expressly agreed terms in one document (or, where contracts are exchanged, in each), and signed by or on behalf of each party.
- A contract that does not comply is void, not merely unenforceable.
- Exceptions (s2(5)) include contracts to grant short leases within s54(2) LPA and sales at public auction.
- Section 2 does not affect the creation or operation of resulting, implied or constructive trusts (s2(5)). In Yaxley v Gotts [2000] Ch 162, an oral agreement under which a builder renovated a house in return for a ground-floor flat was enforced through a constructive trust.

Stage 2: completion by deed
- A conveyance of land or of an interest in land is void for the purpose of conveying or creating a legal estate unless made by deed (LPA s52(1)).
- A deed must make clear on its face that it is intended to be a deed, and be validly executed: signed in the presence of a witness who attests the signature, and delivered (LP(MP)A 1989, s1).
- Exception: a lease taking effect in possession for a term not exceeding three years, at the best rent reasonably obtainable without taking a fine, can be created orally or in writing (LPA s54(2)).

Stage 3: registration
For registered land, registrable dispositions (transfers, leases over seven years, legal charges, express legal easements) do not operate at law until registered (Land Registration Act 2002, s27). Until then the buyer has only an equitable interest.

Equitable interests: LPA s53
- s53(1)(a): an interest in land must be created or disposed of in writing signed by the person creating or conveying it.
- s53(1)(b): a declaration of trust of land must be manifested and proved by signed writing.
- s53(1)(c): a disposition of a subsisting equitable interest must be in signed writing.
- s53(2): these rules do not affect resulting, implied or constructive trusts.

A specifically enforceable contract to grant a lease or other interest gives rise to an equitable interest, because equity treats as done that which ought to be done (Walsh v Lonsdale (1882) 21 Ch D 9).

Proprietary estoppel
Estoppel can create rights without any formality. The elements are: an assurance (or encouragement or acquiescence), reasonable reliance and detriment, so that it would be unconscionable for the owner to go back on the assurance.
- Thorner v Major [2009] UKHL 18: a farmer's conduct over many years, including handing over an insurance notice with the words "that's for my death duties", was a clear enough assurance in context that his relative, who had worked unpaid on the farm for decades, would inherit it.
- Cobbe v Yeoman's Row Management [2008] UKHL 55: a property developer who relied on an agreement in principle that both sides knew was not legally binding could not use estoppel to obtain an interest; he received a payment for his services instead.
- Guest v Guest [2022] UKSC 27 (3-2): the remedy aims to correct the unconscionability of going back on the promise. The usual starting point is to fulfil the claimant's expectation, unless that would be out of all proportion to the detriment, adjusted to avoid over-compensation (for example, for receiving the land earlier than promised). The dissent (Lords Leggatt and Stephens) would have focused on compensating the detriment.
- In registered land, an equity by estoppel is capable of binding successors in title from the time it arises (LRA 2002, s116).

Exam tips: In a problem, follow each transaction through the three stages and identify where it falls short. If formalities fail, look for an equitable route: Walsh v Lonsdale, a constructive trust or proprietary estoppel.

notes.h: Registered land: registration, priority and overriding interests
notes.body:
The Land Registration Act 2002 (LRA) aims to make the register as complete and accurate a record of title as possible, so that a buyer can rely on it with minimal further enquiry. Three ideas are often used to describe the system: the mirror principle (the register reflects the title), the curtain principle (trusts are kept off the register) and the insurance principle (the state compensates those who lose out through errors).

Registration
- Certain events, such as a sale, gift or first legal mortgage of unregistered land, or the grant of a lease of more than seven years, trigger compulsory first registration (s4).
- The registered proprietor is deemed to hold the legal estate, even if the registration was a mistake (s58).

Priority
- The basic rule: a disposition does not affect the priority of an existing interest (s28). Priority is normally first in time.
- The special rule: a registrable disposition of a registered estate for valuable consideration, once completed by registration, takes priority over any interest not protected at the time of registration (s29). Interests are protected if they are entered on the register (for example by a notice), are overriding interests under Schedule 3, or appear from the register to be excepted.
- Interests under a trust of land cannot be protected by a notice (s33). They are protected by a restriction (s40), which ensures overreaching by requiring payment to two trustees, or they may override if the beneficiary is in actual occupation.

Overriding interests on a registered disposition (Schedule 3)
- Para 1: legal leases of seven years or less.
- Para 2: the interest of a person in actual occupation, so far as relating to the land occupied. It does not override if the person failed to disclose it on reasonable enquiry, or if the occupation would not have been obvious on a reasonably careful inspection and the buyer did not actually know of the interest.
- Para 3: legal easements and profits, unless neither known to the buyer nor obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, and not exercised in the year before the disposition.

Key cases on actual occupation
- Williams & Glyn's Bank v Boland [1981] AC 487: a wife who had contributed to the purchase had a beneficial interest and, being in actual occupation, it bound the bank that lent to her husband, the sole registered owner (decided under the Land Registration Act 1925, s70(1)(g)). Because there was only one trustee, the interest was not overreached.
- City of London Building Society v Flegg [1988] AC 54: where mortgage money was paid to two trustees, the occupiers' beneficial interests were overreached, even though they were in actual occupation.
- Abbey National Building Society v Cann [1991] 1 AC 56: the relevant date for actual occupation is completion; preparatory acts such as moving furniture in before completion were not actual occupation. A purchase and the mortgage that funds it are one indivisible transaction, so an occupier claiming through the purchaser cannot take priority over the purchase lender.
- Link Lending v Bustard [2010] EWCA Civ 424: a woman living in a residential care home was still in actual occupation of her house because of her furniture, regular visits and intention to return.

Alteration, rectification and indemnity
The register can be altered to correct mistakes (Schedule 4). Rectification is an alteration that corrects a mistake and prejudicially affects a registered proprietor's title; a proprietor in possession is protected unless he caused or substantially contributed to the mistake by fraud or lack of proper care, or it would be unjust not to rectify. A person who suffers loss through a mistake or rectification may claim an indemnity (Schedule 8), as a lender did after a forged charge in Swift 1st Ltd v Chief Land Registrar [2015] EWCA Civ 330.

Unregistered land
Priority depends on registration of land charges (Land Charges Act 1972). An unregistered estate contract was void against a purchaser for money or money's worth, even one who knew of it and paid well below value (Midland Bank Trust Co v Green [1981] AC 513).

Exam tips: Identify the interest, check whether it was protected on the register and, if not, apply Schedule 3 carefully, including the para 2 exceptions. Always ask whether overreaching has occurred.

Adverse possession allows a person in long-term possession of land without the owner's permission (a "squatter") to acquire title. It is justified by the need to prevent stale claims, to protect long-settled possession and to keep land in use, but it is controversial because an owner can lose land without compensation.

What counts as adverse possession?
Two elements are required (Powell v McFarlane (1977) 38 P & CR 452):
- Factual possession: an appropriate degree of physical control, judged by the nature of the land. Enclosing land, for example by fencing it or locking a gate, is strong evidence.
- Intention to possess: an intention, in one's own name and on one's own behalf, to exclude the world at large, including the paper owner, so far as reasonably practicable.
The possession must be without the owner's consent; possession under a licence is not adverse.

Key cases:
- J A Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2002] UKHL 30: the Grahams grazed land under an agreement that expired; Pye refused to renew it but the Grahams kept using the land for more than 12 years. The House of Lords held that what is required is an intention to possess, not an intention to own, and that the squatters' willingness to pay for a licence did not defeat it. Pye lost land worth millions. The Grand Chamber of the European Court of Human Rights later held that the English rules did not breach Article 1 of Protocol 1 (J A Pye (Oxford) Ltd v UK (2008) 46 EHRR 45).
- Buckinghamshire County Council v Moran [1990] Ch 623: the owner's plans for future use of the land do not prevent the squatter's possession being adverse.
- Best v Chief Land Registrar [2015] EWCA Civ 17: the fact that squatting in a residential building is a criminal offence (LASPO 2012, s144) does not by itself prevent a claim to adverse possession.

Unregistered land
Under the Limitation Act 1980 (s15), the owner's right to recover land is barred after 12 years of adverse possession, and the owner's title is extinguished (s17). The squatter's own possessory title then becomes unchallengeable.

Registered land: Land Registration Act 2002, Schedule 6
The 2002 Act made it much harder for squatters to succeed against registered owners. Limitation no longer runs against a registered estate (s96).
- After 10 years' adverse possession, the squatter may apply to be registered (para 1).
- The registered proprietor and others are notified and can object (para 2).
- If anyone objects, the squatter succeeds only if one of three conditions in para 5 applies:
  - estoppel: it would be unconscionable for the owner to evict the squatter, and the squatter ought to be registered;
  - some other right: the squatter is entitled to the land for another reason, for example a buyer who paid but never received a transfer;
  - boundary: the land is adjacent to the squatter's land, the exact boundary has not been fixed, the squatter reasonably believed for at least 10 years that the land was his, and the estate was registered more than a year before the application. Zarb v Parry [2011] EWCA Civ 1306 is an example.
- If the application is rejected but the squatter remains in adverse possession for a further two years, he can apply again and will then be registered (paras 6-7). This gives the owner two years to evict.

Transitional rule: squatters who had completed 12 years against a registered owner before the Act came into force on 13 October 2003 keep their accrued rights.

Exam tips: Separate factual possession, intention to possess and lack of consent. Then decide whether the land is registered or unregistered and apply the correct scheme. Comment on whether the 2002 Act strikes the right balance.

Whenever two or more people own land concurrently there is a trust of land: trustees hold the legal estate and beneficiaries the equitable interests, and they are often the same people.

Joint tenancy and tenancy in common
- In a joint tenancy, each co-owner owns the whole and there are no shares. The right of survivorship applies: when a joint tenant dies, the survivors take the whole. It requires the four unities of possession, interest, title and time.
- In a tenancy in common, each owns a distinct but undivided share (e.g. 60:40), which passes under their will or intestacy.
- The legal estate can only be held on a joint tenancy (LPA ss1(6), 34 and 36(2)), and by no more than four trustees. This keeps the legal title simple for buyers.
- In equity, co-owners may be joint tenants or tenants in common. Words of severance in the transfer ("equally", "in shares") create a tenancy in common. Equity also presumes a tenancy in common in some cases, for example where business partners buy land (Malayan Credit v Jack Chia-MPH [1986] AC 549).

Severance
Only a beneficial joint tenancy can be severed, turning it into a tenancy in common.
- Written notice under LPA s36(2). In Kinch v Bullard [1999] 1 WLR 423, a notice was effectively served when delivered to the husband's address, even though the wife who sent it then destroyed it after he fell ill. A notice must show a desire to sever immediately: a general request in a divorce petition for property orders in the future was not enough (Harris v Goddard [1983] 1 WLR 1203).
- The three methods in Williams v Hensman (1861) 1 J & H 546: an act operating on one's own share (such as selling or mortgaging it); mutual agreement; or a course of dealing showing a common intention to treat the interests as several.
- Burgess v Rawnsley [1975] Ch 429: an oral agreement for one co-owner to buy out the other severed the joint tenancy, even though it was later abandoned and was not an enforceable contract.

The Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996 (TOLATA)
- Trustees have the powers of an absolute owner (s6), and must consult adult beneficiaries entitled to an interest in possession (s11).
- Beneficiaries entitled to an interest in possession have a right to occupy if the purposes of the trust include occupation and the land is available and suitable (s12). Trustees may exclude or restrict occupation by some beneficiaries and impose conditions such as compensation payments (s13).
- Any trustee or person with an interest in the property, including a secured creditor, may apply to the court for an order, for example for sale (s14).
- In deciding, the court must consider the intentions of the person who created the trust, the purposes for which the property is held, the welfare of any minor who occupies it, and the interests of any secured creditor of a beneficiary (s15).
- In Mortgage Corporation v Shaire [2001] Ch 743, the court held that s15 changed the law: a creditor's interests are no longer automatically paramount. Even so, in Bank of Ireland Home Mortgages v Bell [2001] 2 FLR 809, the creditor's interest in being repaid was a powerful factor and sale was ordered.
- Where a beneficiary is bankrupt, Insolvency Act 1986 s335A applies instead: after a year, the creditors' interests are assumed to outweigh all other considerations unless the circumstances are exceptional.

Overreaching
When trustees sell or mortgage and the capital money is paid to at least two trustees (or a trust corporation), the beneficial interests are overreached: they detach from the land and attach to the proceeds (LPA ss2 and 27). The buyer or lender takes free of them (City of London Building Society v Flegg [1988] AC 54). Overreaching can occur even where no capital money is paid at the time, for example on a mortgage securing existing debts (State Bank of India v Sood [1997] Ch 276).

Exam tips: Separate the legal title from the beneficial interests, test each possible severance against s36(2) and Williams v Hensman, and use ss14-15 (or s335A) for disputes about sale.

notes.h: Beneficial ownership of the family home
notes.body:
Disputes about who owns the family home typically arise when unmarried couples separate (married couples usually rely on the court's statutory powers on divorce). The question is how the beneficial interest is shared, which depends on whether the home is in joint names or one name.

Express declarations
If the parties have expressly declared their beneficial shares in signed writing (LPA s53(1)(b)), the declaration is normally conclusive, absent fraud, mistake or a later variation (Goodman v Gallant [1986] Fam 106; Pankhania v Chandegra [2012] EWCA Civ 1438). Lawyers' failure to complete the declaration on the transfer form is what produces many disputes.

Resulting trusts
Traditionally, a person who contributed to the purchase price was presumed to take a share in proportion to their contribution. In the domestic context the resulting trust has largely been replaced by the common intention constructive trust, which looks at the parties' whole relationship (Stack v Dowden).

Joint names cases
- Stack v Dowden [2007] UKHL 17: an unmarried couple bought a house in joint names without declaring their shares; Ms Dowden had contributed significantly more. The House of Lords held that equity follows the law, so the starting point is a beneficial joint tenancy. The party claiming unequal shares must show that the parties intended otherwise, judged from their whole course of dealing in relation to the property. This will be unusual. On the facts, Ms Dowden was entitled to 65%.
- Jones v Kernott [2011] UKSC 53: the couple bought in joint names; after separation, Ms Jones paid all the outgoings for many years. The Supreme Court held that the presumption of equal shares can be displaced by showing a different common intention, either when the property was bought or later. If the parties intended their shares to change but it is impossible to infer what shares they intended, the court may impute an intention, awarding what is fair having regard to the whole course of dealing. The Supreme Court restored the trial judge's decision giving Ms Jones 90%.

Sole name cases
The claimant must first prove that the parties had a common intention that the claimant should have a beneficial share, and that they relied on it to their detriment.
- Lloyds Bank v Rosset [1991] 1 AC 107: Lord Bridge said this common intention could be shown by express discussions (however imprecise) plus detrimental reliance, or inferred from conduct, in which case direct contributions to the purchase price would readily justify the inference and it was "extremely doubtful whether anything less will do". Mrs Rosset's work renovating the house did not suffice.
- Express discussions can include excuses that imply a shared understanding, as where a man told his partner that her name was not on the title only because she was too young (Eves v Eves [1975] 1 WLR 1338) or because it might prejudice her divorce proceedings (Grant v Edwards [1986] Ch 638).
- In Stack, Baroness Hale suggested that Lord Bridge's view may have set the hurdle too high. Later cases look at the whole course of dealing when quantifying shares in sole name cases too (Abbott v Abbott [2007] UKPC 53).
- But the existence of a common intention to share in a sole name case cannot be imputed; it must be actual, express or inferred (Geary v Rankine [2012] EWCA Civ 555). Imputation is only available at the quantification stage.
- In Marr v Collie [2017] UKPC 17 the Privy Council held that the Stack approach is not confined to domestic homes and may apply to investment properties bought by a couple, depending on the context.

Proprietary estoppel overlaps with the constructive trust, but the remedy is more flexible.

Reform
The Law Commission recommended a statutory scheme for cohabitants in 2007 (Law Com No 307). At the time of writing (November 2026) it has not been implemented, although the government opened a consultation on cohabitation reform in June 2026, so the trusts approach still governs. Check the latest position.

Exam tips: Start by asking whose name the legal title is in and whether there is an express declaration. Then apply Stack and Kernott (joint names) or the two-stage approach of acquisition then quantification (sole name). Distinguish inference (finding the actual intention) from imputation (attributing an intention the court thinks fair).

A lease (term of years absolute) is one of only two legal estates. It gives the tenant a proprietary right that can bind purchasers of the landlord's interest, unlike a licence, which is personal.

Essential characteristics
- Exclusive possession: the right to exclude everyone, including the landlord.
- A term certain: the maximum duration must be known from the start.
- Rent is usual but not essential (LPA s205(1)(xxvii); Ashburn Anstalt v Arnold [1989] Ch 1).

Lease or licence?
Street v Mountford [1985] AC 809: Mrs Mountford signed an agreement called a "licence" for two rooms. The House of Lords held that where residential accommodation is granted for a term at a rent with exclusive possession, the grant is a tenancy, whatever label the parties use, unless there is a special reason (for example, a service occupancy, an act of friendship or generosity, or no intention to create legal relations). Lord Templeman said that a five-pronged implement for digging is a fork even if its maker calls it a spade.

Sham terms and sharers: AG Securities v Vaughan; Antoniades v Villiers [1990] 1 AC 417.
- In AG Securities, four people who moved into a flat at different times on separate agreements had licences, as there was no joint exclusive possession.
- In Antoniades, a couple sharing a small flat signed separate "licences" that let the owner introduce other occupiers. The clause was a pretence, never intended to be used, and they were joint tenants.

Certainty of term
- Lace v Chantler [1944] KB 368: a lease "for the duration of the war" was void for uncertainty.
- Prudential Assurance v London Residuary Body [1992] 2 AC 386: a lease until land was needed for road widening was uncertain, but the payment and acceptance of yearly rent created a yearly periodic tenancy.
- Berrisford v Mexfield Housing Co-operative [2011] UKSC 52: an agreement that could be ended by the co-operative only on specified grounds was uncertain as a term, but because it would have been a lease for life before 1926, it took effect under LPA s149(6) as a 90-year lease determinable on Ms Berrisford's death.
- Periodic tenancies (weekly, monthly, yearly) are valid because each period is certain.

Non-proprietary leases
In Bruton v London & Quadrant Housing Trust [2000] 1 AC 406, a housing trust that was only a licensee granted Mr Bruton exclusive possession; this was a tenancy between the parties, so statutory repairing obligations applied, even though the trust had no estate.

Formalities and registration
- A legal lease needs a deed (s52) unless within s54(2) (three years or less, in possession, best rent, no fine).
- Leases of more than seven years must be registered to take effect at law (LRA 2002, s27(2)(b)).
- Legal leases of seven years or less override under Schedule 3 para 1.
- An informal lease may take effect as an equitable lease (Walsh v Lonsdale).

Leasehold covenants
- For leases granted on or after 1 January 1996, the Landlord and Tenant (Covenants) Act 1995 applies. Benefits and burdens of covenants (other than personal ones) pass on assignment (s3). The original tenant is released on a lawful assignment (s5), although he may be required to guarantee his immediate assignee under an authorised guarantee agreement (s16).
- For older leases, covenants that "touch and concern" the land pass with the lease and reversion (P & A Swift Investments v Combined English Stores [1989] AC 632), but the original tenant stays liable for the whole term.

Forfeiture
A landlord can forfeit only if the lease contains a right of re-entry. For breaches other than non-payment of rent, a notice under LPA s146 is required, and the tenant can seek relief. Where premises are let as a dwelling, a right of re-entry cannot be enforced except by court proceedings while anyone is lawfully residing there (Protection from Eviction Act 1977, s2).

Residential tenancies today
Statute heavily regulates residential lettings. At the time of writing (November 2026), the main reforms in the Renters' Rights Act 2025 have applied in England since 1 May 2026: assured shorthold tenancies have been replaced by periodic assured tenancies and "no-fault" section 21 evictions have been abolished. Check the latest position.

Exam tips: Test exclusive possession, then term certainty, then any Street v Mountford exception. For third parties, check the lease's length, formalities and registration.

An easement is a proprietary right over one piece of land (the servient tenement) for the benefit of another (the dominant tenement), such as a right of way, light or drainage.

Requirements: Re Ellenborough Park [1956] Ch 131
Houses around a park were sold with the right to use the park as a pleasure ground. The Court of Appeal held that this was an easement and set out four requirements:
- There must be a dominant and a servient tenement.
- The right must accommodate the dominant tenement: it must benefit the land and its normal use, not just the owner personally. In Hill v Tupper (1863) a boating monopoly benefited a business, not the land.
- The dominant and servient owners must be different persons.
- The right must be capable of forming the subject matter of a grant: there must be a capable grantor and grantee, the right must be sufficiently definite, and it must be of a kind recognised as an easement.

Limits on what can be an easement
- No right to a view or to general protection from the weather (Phipps v Pears [1965] 1 QB 76).
- Ouster: a right that leaves the servient owner without reasonable use of the land cannot be an easement. Storing cars on a strip of land was too extensive in Copeland v Greenhalf [1952] Ch 488, and a right to park six cars in a space for six during the working week failed in Batchelor v Marlow [2001] EWCA Civ 1051. In Moncrieff v Jamieson [2007] UKHL 42 (a Scottish case), Lord Scott suggested, obiter, replacing the reasonable-use test with one asking whether the servient owner retains possession and control; Lord Neuberger saw force in this but reached no concluded view, and Batchelor v Marlow was not overruled. At the time of writing (November 2026), the Supreme Court had heard an appeal on the correct ouster test (Stenner v Teignbridge District Council, heard 22 July 2026) and judgment was awaited; check whether it has been decided.
- Recreational rights: in Regency Villas Title Ltd v Diamond Resorts (Europe) Ltd [2018] UKSC 57, the Supreme Court (Lord Carnwath dissenting) held that a right to use a swimming pool, golf course, squash courts and other sporting facilities on neighbouring land was a valid easement for timeshare owners. Purely recreational rights can accommodate the dominant land where that land is itself used for leisure. The rights required only passivity from the servient owner, who was under no duty to maintain or run the facilities, so the rule against easements requiring the servient owner to spend money did not defeat them. Lord Carnwath would have held that rights to use a golf course or pool cannot be enjoyed without the owner actively running them.

Creation
- Express grant or reservation, by deed. In registered land an express legal easement must be completed by registration (LRA 2002, s27(2)(d)); otherwise it is equitable.
- Implied by necessity, where land would otherwise be inaccessible (Nickerson v Barraclough [1981] Ch 426).
- Implied by common intention, to give effect to the purpose for which land was sold (Wong v Beaumont Property Trust [1965] 1 QB 173, ventilation duct for a restaurant).
- Wheeldon v Burrows (1879) 12 Ch D 31: on a sale of part, the buyer gets rights that the common owner was using (quasi-easements) that are continuous and apparent, necessary for the reasonable enjoyment of the part sold, and in use at the time of the sale.
- LPA s62: a conveyance passes with the land all rights and advantages appertaining to it, which can turn a permission (licence) into an easement (Wright v Macadam [1949] 2 KB 744, coal shed). Traditionally this required prior diversity of occupation (Long v Gowlett [1923] 2 Ch 177), but not where the right was continuous and apparent (P & S Platt v Crouch [2003] EWCA Civ 1110; Wood v Waddington [2015] EWCA Civ 538).
- Prescription: 20 years' use as of right (without force, secrecy or permission), by common law, lost modern grant (Dalton v Angus (1881)) or the Prescription Act 1832.

Easements and registered land
Implied and prescriptive legal easements can override a registered disposition under Schedule 3 para 3, but only if known to the buyer, obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, or exercised within the year before the disposition.

Reform
The Law Commission's proposals in Making Land Work (Law Com No 327, 2011) have not been implemented.

Exam tips: Apply the Ellenborough requirements, then the method of creation, then whether the easement binds the current servient owner.

A freehold covenant is a promise by one landowner to another about the use of land, for example not to build more than one house, or to maintain a fence. The main question is whether the covenant binds and benefits later owners of the land.

Restrictive and positive covenants
- A restrictive (negative) covenant restricts the use of land, e.g. not to use the land for business. The test is substance, not wording: a covenant that requires spending money or doing something is positive (Haywood v Brunswick Permanent Benefit Building Society (1881)).
- A positive covenant requires the owner to do something or spend money, e.g. to repair a roof or contribute to road costs.

The burden
- At common law, the burden of a covenant does not run with freehold land (Austerberry v Oldham Corporation (1885) 29 Ch D 750).
- In equity, the burden of a restrictive covenant can run under Tulk v Moxhay (1848) 2 Ph 774, where a purchaser with notice of a covenant to keep Leicester Square garden open was bound. The requirements are:
  - the covenant must be negative in substance;
  - it must have been made to benefit land retained by the covenantee (London County Council v Allen [1914] 3 KB 642);
  - the original parties must have intended the burden to run (presumed by LPA s79 unless excluded); and
  - the covenant must be protected: by a notice on the register in registered land, or as a Class D(ii) land charge in unregistered land (for post-1925 covenants).
- The burden of a positive covenant does not run in equity either: Rhone v Stephens [1994] 2 AC 310, where a covenant to repair a roof did not bind a later owner. The House of Lords refused to depart from Austerberry, saying change was for Parliament.

Getting around the positive covenant rule
- Benefit and burden: a person who takes the benefit of a right must accept a reciprocal burden that is relevant to it (Halsall v Brizell [1957] Ch 169, paying for roads and drains used). The burden must be linked to the benefit, and the successor must have a real choice whether to take the benefit (Thamesmead Town Ltd v Allotey (1998) 30 HLR 1052).
- A chain of indemnity covenants.
- Granting long leases instead of freeholds, since leasehold covenants run under the 1995 Act.
- Commonhold (Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Act 2002), which has had little take-up.
- An estate rentcharge with a right of entry.

The benefit
- At law, the benefit can pass if the covenant touches and concerns the land, the original covenantee held a legal estate, the successor holds a legal estate, and it was intended to run (LPA s78).
- In equity, the benefit passes by:
  - annexation: express words, or statutory annexation under s78. In Federated Homes v Mill Lodge Properties [1980] 1 WLR 594, the Court of Appeal held that s78 annexes the benefit of a covenant relating to the land of the covenantee to each and every part of that land. The land must be identifiable from the covenant (Crest Nicholson Residential v McAllister [2004] EWCA Civ 410);
  - express assignment; or
  - a building scheme, where an estate is laid out in plots subject to common covenants intended to be mutually enforceable (Elliston v Reacher [1908] 2 Ch 374).

Discharge and modification
The Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) can discharge or modify restrictive covenants under LPA s84, for example where they are obsolete or impede reasonable use contrary to the public interest. In Alexander Devine Children's Cancer Trust v Housing Solutions Ltd [2020] UKSC 45, a developer had built houses in deliberate breach of a covenant. The Upper Tribunal had modified the covenant; the Court of Appeal reversed that, and the Supreme Court dismissed the further appeal, so modification was refused: the developer's cynical conduct was relevant to the tribunal's discretion, and it should not benefit from presenting a fait accompli.

Reform
The Law Commission recommended allowing positive obligations to run with land (Law Com No 327, 2011), but this has not been implemented.

Exam tips: Treat burden and benefit separately. For burden, ask: positive or restrictive? Tulk v Moxhay requirements met? Registered? For benefit: original covenantee or successor? Annexation, assignment or scheme?

A mortgage is security for a loan. The borrower (mortgagor) keeps ownership, while the lender (mortgagee) gets a proprietary right to enforce the debt against the land.

Creation
- Since 1925 a legal mortgage of freehold land is created either by a long lease (now obsolete) or by a charge by deed expressed to be by way of legal mortgage (LPA ss85-87). For registered land, the only method is a charge (LRA 2002, s23), which must be registered to take effect at law (s27(2)(f)).
- Registered charges rank in the order shown on the register (s48).
- Equitable mortgages arise, for example, from a mortgage of an equitable interest or from an informal mortgage that equity enforces.

The equity of redemption
Equity protects the borrower's right to redeem the property on repaying the debt. "Once a mortgage, always a mortgage": the courts strike down "clogs" that stop the borrower getting the property back free of the mortgage.
- An option for the lender to buy the property, granted as part of the mortgage, is void (Samuel v Jarrah Timber [1904] AC 323), but an option granted in a separate, later transaction may be valid (Reeve v Lisle [1902] AC 461).
- Postponing redemption: a 40-year postponement between commercial parties at arm's length was valid in Knightsbridge Estates Trust v Byrne [1939] Ch 441, but a postponement that made redemption illusory was void in Fairclough v Swan Brewery [1912] AC 565.
- Collateral advantages: a term giving the lender a commercial benefit that survives redemption may be valid if it is not unfair or unconscionable and is not a clog on redemption (Kreglinger v New Patagonia Meat and Cold Storage [1914] AC 25).

Undue influence and surety transactions
Where a person (often a wife) mortgages her interest in the home to secure someone else's debts (often her husband's business), she may later claim the transaction was procured by undue influence or misrepresentation.
- Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2001] UKHL 44: a lender is put on inquiry whenever the relationship between surety and debtor is non-commercial. To protect itself, the lender should communicate directly with the surety, ask her to nominate a solicitor, provide the solicitor with the necessary financial information, and obtain the solicitor's confirmation that the surety has been advised. If it does so, it can rely on the transaction.
- A joint loan for the couple's joint benefit does not put the lender on inquiry (CIBC Mortgages v Pitt [1994] 1 AC 200).

The lender's remedies
- Possession: the lender has a right to possession as soon as the mortgage is made, unless excluded (Four-Maids Ltd v Dudley Marshall [1957] Ch 317). For dwelling houses, the court may adjourn or suspend possession if the borrower is likely to be able to pay the sums due within a reasonable period (Administration of Justice Act 1970, s36, as extended by AJA 1973, s8). In Cheltenham & Gloucester BS v Norgan [1996] 1 WLR 343, the court said the starting point for a reasonable period is the remaining term of the mortgage. Section 36 applies only to court proceedings, so a lender may take possession of an empty property without a court order (Ropaigealach v Barclays Bank [2000] QB 263).
- Sale: the statutory power arises when the mortgage money is due (LPA s101) and becomes exercisable on default as set out in s103 (e.g. three months after notice requiring repayment, or interest two months in arrears). The lender must act in good faith and take reasonable care to obtain the true market value at the time it chooses to sell (Cuckmere Brick v Mutual Finance [1971] Ch 949), but it can choose when to sell (Silven Properties v Royal Bank of Scotland [2003] EWCA Civ 1409). Any surplus after paying the debt is held on trust for the borrower (s105).
- The court can order sale even at the borrower's request and against the lender's wishes (LPA s91(2); Palk v Mortgage Services Funding [1993] Ch 330).
- Appointing a receiver to collect rents (s109).

Exam tips: For clogs, separate options, postponement and collateral advantages. Apply the Etridge steps in surety cases, and distinguish possession from sale when discussing enforcement.

cards.b: A personal right binds only the grantor; a proprietary right is a right in the land, capable of binding third parties and surviving the grantor's insolvency.
A deserted wife's 'equity' was personal, not proprietary. A property right must be definable, identifiable by third parties, capable of assumption by them and have some permanence or stability.
Only two legal estates: the fee simple absolute in possession and the term of years absolute.
Legal interests include easements equivalent to a legal estate and charges by way of legal mortgage (s1(2)); all other estates and interests are equitable (s1(3)).
An exclusive right to put pleasure boats on a canal was a personal licence, not an easement: the law will not allow new property rights to be invented freely.
A contractual licence to put up advertising was personal and did not bind a later purchaser of the land.
Court of Appeal: a contractual licence is not an interest in land, but a constructive trust may bind a purchaser whose conscience is affected.
A bungalow resting on pillars that could only be removed by destroying it was part of the land, not a chattel.

A contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land must be in writing, incorporate all expressly agreed terms in one document (or each exchanged part) and be signed by each party; otherwise void.
A conveyance of land or an interest in land is void for the purpose of conveying or creating a legal estate unless made by deed.
A lease taking effect in possession for up to three years, at the best rent reasonably obtainable without a fine, can be created without a deed or writing.
Clear on its face that it is a deed; signed in the presence of an attesting witness; and delivered.
A specifically enforceable contract for a lease creates an equitable lease on the same terms, because equity treats as done that which ought to be done.
An assurance can be inferred from conduct over many years if clear enough in context; a relative who worked unpaid on a farm for decades established proprietary estoppel.
No proprietary estoppel where a commercial party relied on an agreement both sides knew was not legally binding; he got payment for his work instead.

Estoppel remedy aims to cure the unconscionability of resiling from the promise; starting point is to fulfil the expectation unless out of all proportion to the detriment, adjusted for early receipt. Decided 3-2.

A registrable disposition for valuable consideration, completed by registration, takes priority over interests not protected (by notice, as overriding, or as excepted on the register) at the time of registration.

Interest of a person in actual occupation overrides, unless not disclosed on reasonable enquiry, or occupation not obvious on reasonably careful inspection and the buyer did not actually know of the interest.
A wife's beneficial interest, with actual occupation, bound the bank lending to her husband, the sole registered owner; no overreaching as there was one trustee.

cards.f: City of London BS v Flegg [1988]
cards.b: Payment of mortgage money to two trustees overreached the beneficiaries' interests even though they were in actual occupation.
Actual occupation is tested at completion; moving furniture in beforehand is not occupation. Purchase and acquisition mortgage are one indivisible transaction.
A woman in residential care remained in actual occupation of her home given her furniture, regular visits and intention to return.
Mirror (register reflects title), curtain (trusts kept off the register, protected by overreaching) and insurance (state indemnity for loss through register errors).

cards.f: Midland Bank Trust Co v Green [1981]
cards.b: Unregistered land: an unregistered option (estate contract) was void against a purchaser for money or money's worth, despite knowledge and a low price.
Adverse possession requires factual possession (appropriate physical control) and intention to possess (to exclude the world, including the paper owner, so far as reasonably practicable).

cards.f: J A Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2002]
cards.b: House of Lords: intention to possess, not to own, is required; a squatter's willingness to pay for a licence does not defeat it.

cards.f: J A Pye (Oxford) Ltd v UK (2008)
cards.b: Grand Chamber of the ECtHR: the English adverse possession rules did not violate Article 1 of Protocol 1.
Unregistered land: the owner's action to recover land is barred after 12 years of adverse possession, and title is extinguished.
A squatter with 10 years' adverse possession of registered land may apply to be registered; the registered proprietor is notified and can object.
If the owner objects, the squatter succeeds only on: estoppel; some other right to the land; or the boundary condition (adjacent land, reasonable belief for 10 years).
If the first application is rejected and the squatter stays in adverse possession for a further two years, he may reapply and must be registered.
The criminal offence of squatting in a residential building (LASPO 2012, s144) does not in itself bar an adverse possession claim.

cards.f: Joint tenancy v tenancy in common
cards.b: Joint tenancy: each owns the whole, no shares, survivorship applies, four unities needed. Tenancy in common: distinct undivided shares that pass on death by will or intestacy.
Must be held as a joint tenancy (LPA ss1(6), 34, 36(2)) by no more than four trustees; beneficial interests may be joint or in common.
A severance notice under s36(2) was validly served when delivered to the co-owner's address, even though the sender then destroyed it.
Severance in equity by: an act operating on one's own share; mutual agreement; or a mutual course of dealing.
An oral agreement for one joint tenant to buy the other's share severed the joint tenancy even though it was not enforceable and was later abandoned.
Court considers: the settlor's intentions; the purposes for which the land is held; welfare of any minor occupying; and the interests of any secured creditor of a beneficiary.
Under s15 TOLATA, a secured creditor's interests are not automatically paramount; the court weighs all the s15 factors.
Where capital money is paid to at least two trustees or a trust corporation, beneficial interests detach from the land and attach to the proceeds; the buyer or lender takes free.
An express declaration of beneficial shares in signed writing is conclusive, absent fraud, mistake or later variation.
Joint names: equity follows the law, so beneficial joint tenancy is presumed; the claimant must show a different common intention from the whole course of dealing. Ms Dowden received 65%.
Joint names: the common intention may change over time; if shares cannot be inferred, the court may impute fair shares. Trial judge's 90:10 split for Ms Jones restored.
Sole name: common intention shown by express discussion plus detrimental reliance, or inferred from conduct (direct contributions); renovation work was not enough.

cards.f: Eves v Eves [1975] / Grant v Edwards [1986]
cards.b: Excuses for not putting a partner on the title (too young; would prejudice divorce) were evidence of an express common intention to share.
In a sole name case, the existence of a common intention to share cannot be imputed; it must be actual. Imputation is allowed only to quantify shares.
Inference: deducing the parties' actual intention from conduct. Imputation: attributing an intention the parties never had, based on what is fair (Kernott).
Privy Council: the Stack approach is not confined to the family home and can apply to investment properties bought by a couple, depending on context.
Exclusive possession for a term at a rent creates a tenancy whatever the label, unless a special exception applies (e.g. service occupancy, generosity, no intention to create legal relations).

cards.f: AG Securities v Vaughan; Antoniades v Villiers [1990]
cards.b: Separate agreements with no joint exclusive possession were licences (AG Securities); a clause letting the owner introduce others into a couple's flat was a pretence, so they were joint tenants (Antoniades).
A lease 'for the duration of the war' was void because its maximum duration was uncertain.

cards.f: Prudential Assurance v London Residuary Body [1992]
cards.b: A term until land was required for road widening was uncertain, but payment of yearly rent created a yearly periodic tenancy.
An uncertain occupancy agreement took effect under LPA s149(6) as a 90-year lease determinable on the occupier's death, because before 1926 it would have been a lease for life.
A grantor with no estate can create a tenancy binding between the parties (a non-proprietary lease); here, statutory repairing obligations applied.
For leases from 1 Jan 1996: non-personal covenants pass on assignment (s3); original tenant released on assignment (s5), subject to an authorised guarantee agreement (s16).
Main reforms in force in England from 1 May 2026: assured shorthold tenancies replaced by periodic assured tenancies; section 21 'no-fault' evictions abolished. Check the latest position.
Dominant and servient tenement; right accommodates dominant land; different owners; capable of forming the subject matter of a grant.
The right must benefit the dominant land and its normal use, not just the owner personally or a business (contrast Hill v Tupper).

cards.f: Regency Villas v Diamond Resorts [2018] UKSC 57
cards.b: Supreme Court: purely recreational and sporting rights (pool, golf course, courts) can be easements; the servient owner need only be passive and has no duty to run or maintain them. Lord Carnwath dissented.

A right that leaves the servient owner without reasonable use of the land cannot be an easement (Copeland v Greenhalf; Batchelor v Marlow). Supreme Court judgment on the test awaited in Nov 2026 (Stenner).
On sale of part, quasi-easements pass if continuous and apparent, necessary for reasonable enjoyment, and in use by the common owner at the time of sale.

A conveyance passes all rights and advantages appertaining to the land; can convert a licence into an easement (Wright v Macadam). Diversity of occupation not needed if continuous and apparent (Wood v Waddington).
20 years' use as of right (without force, secrecy or permission): common law, lost modern grant or Prescription Act 1832.
Implied or prescriptive legal easements override only if known to the buyer, obvious on reasonably careful inspection, or exercised in the year before the disposition.
The burden of a restrictive covenant runs in equity to a successor with notice (now, if protected by registration); the Leicester Square garden case.
The burden of a covenant does not run with freehold land at common law.
The burden of a positive covenant (to repair a roof) does not run in equity either; the House of Lords left reform to Parliament.

cards.f: Requirements for burden to run in equity
cards.b: Negative in substance; made to benefit land retained by covenantee; intended to run (s79 LPA); protected by registration (notice or Class D(ii) land charge).
A successor who takes the benefit of a right (roads, drains) must accept the related burden (contributing to costs).
s78 LPA annexes the benefit of a covenant relating to the covenantee's land to every part of that land, without express words.
Statutory annexation under s78 requires that the benefited land be identifiable from the covenant document.

Developer built in cynical breach of a covenant. The Upper Tribunal modified it under s84 LPA; the Court of Appeal reversed and the Supreme Court dismissed the further appeal. The breach counted at the discretionary stage.

cards.f: Charge by way of legal mortgage
cards.b: Created by deed (LPA ss85-87); for registered land the only form of legal mortgage, which must be registered to take effect at law (LRA ss23, 27).
An option for the lender to buy the mortgaged property, granted as part of the mortgage, is a void clog on the equity of redemption.
A 40-year postponement of redemption agreed between commercial parties at arm's length was valid.
A collateral advantage that survives redemption can be valid if it is not unfair or unconscionable and is not a clog on redemption.
Lender put on inquiry whenever a surety's relationship with the debtor is non-commercial; it should deal directly with the surety and get a solicitor's confirmation of advice.
For a dwelling house, the court may adjourn or suspend possession if the borrower is likely to pay the sums due within a reasonable period (extended by AJA 1973, s8).
The starting point for a 'reasonable period' under s36 is the remaining term of the mortgage.
A lender selling under its power of sale must take reasonable care to obtain the true market value at the time of sale; it may choose when to sell (Silven [2003]).

questions.q: Which of these is capable of existing as a legal estate under s1(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925?
options: A beneficial interest under a trust of land
A life interest in a house
A restrictive covenant
A 99-year lease
questions.why: A 99-year lease is a term of years absolute, one of only two legal estates. Life interests were legal estates before 1926 but can now exist only in equity under s1(3). A restrictive covenant is an interest, not an estate, and takes effect only in equity. Beneficial interests under a trust are by definition equitable.

questions.q: Why did the deserted wife's right to remain in the home not bind the bank in National Provincial Bank v Ainsworth [1965]?
options: The bank was a bona fide purchaser without notice, which defeats even legal rights
Only legal estates can bind third parties
It was a personal right, not sufficiently definable, identifiable and stable to be proprietary
It had not been registered under the Land Registration Act 2002
questions.why: The House of Lords held the right was personal, so it could not bind anyone other than the husband. The 2002 Act did not exist in 1965, so non-registration under it cannot be the reason. The bona fide purchaser doctrine defeats only equitable rights; legal rights bind the world regardless of notice. Equitable interests can and do bind third parties, so the claim that only legal estates bind them is wrong.

questions.q: Explain the difference between personal and proprietary rights in land, and why it matters.
markScheme: Defines personal rights (binding only the grantor) and proprietary rights (rights in the land)
Explains consequence: proprietary rights can bind third parties and survive insolvency
Ainsworth criteria for proprietary status
Example of personal right: contractual licence (King v David Allen; Ashburn Anstalt)
Links to priority and the need for protection (registration)
questions.modelAnswer: A personal right is enforceable only against the person who granted it, for example under a contract. A proprietary right is a right in the land itself, so it is capable of binding third parties who later acquire the land and survives the grantor's insolvency. This matters because land law is largely about priority between competing claims to the same land. In National Provincial Bank v Ainsworth [1965] Lord Wilberforce said a right can only be proprietary if it is definable, identifiable by third parties, capable in its nature of assumption by third parties, and has some degree of permanence or stability; the deserted wife's right to stay in the home failed this test, so it did not bind the bank. Licences are the classic personal right: in King v David Allen [1916] a contractual licence did not bind a purchaser, and Ashburn Anstalt v Arnold [1989] confirmed that contractual licences are not interests in land. Even a proprietary right must usually be protected, for example by registration, to bind a purchaser of registered land.

questions.q: Ann and Ben agree orally that Ben will buy Ann's freehold house for £400,000. Ben pays a deposit. Ann then refuses to proceed. What is the position?
options: There is a binding contract because s2 does not apply to freehold sales
There is no contract, because a contract for the sale of land must be in signed writing incorporating all the terms
There is a valid contract, but it is unenforceable until Ben signs a memorandum
There is a valid contract because Ben has partly performed it
questions.why: Section 2 of the 1989 Act makes a non-compliant contract void, so Ben has no contract (though he may recover his deposit). The 'unenforceable until a memorandum' idea comes from the old s40 LPA 1925, which the 1989 Act replaced. The doctrine of part performance was likewise abolished with s40. Section 2 applies to any contract for the sale or other disposition of an interest in land, including freehold sales.

questions.q: Cal is granted a five-year lease of a flat in a document signed by both parties but not executed as a deed. Assuming the agreement is specifically enforceable, what does Cal have?
options: A legal lease, because the lease is in signed writing
An equitable lease under the doctrine in Walsh v Lonsdale
A legal lease under s54(2) LPA 1925
Nothing, because a void legal lease cannot take effect in any way
questions.why: A five-year lease needs a deed to be legal (s52), but signed writing satisfying s2 of the 1989 Act is a contract that equity treats as an equitable lease (Walsh v Lonsdale). Signed writing alone is not a deed, so the lease cannot be legal. Section 54(2) covers only leases of up to three years. The idea that nothing survives ignores equity's response to a specifically enforceable contract.

questions.q: Outline the requirements of proprietary estoppel and how the court chooses a remedy.
markScheme: Assurance (including by conduct or acquiescence), clear enough in context (Thorner v Major)
Reasonable reliance and detriment
Unconscionability; limits where parties knew agreement not binding (Cobbe)
Remedy: Guest v Guest [2022], starting point is expectation unless out of all proportion to the detriment, adjusted for early receipt
Effect in registered land: s116 LRA 2002
questions.modelAnswer: Proprietary estoppel arises where an owner gives an assurance that the claimant has or will acquire an interest in land, the claimant reasonably relies on it to their detriment, and it would be unconscionable for the owner to go back on it. The assurance may be express or inferred from conduct, provided it is clear enough in its context: in Thorner v Major [2009] years of hints and conduct were enough for a farmer's relative who worked unpaid for decades. Detriment can be financial or personal, such as giving up other opportunities. Estoppel is more difficult in commercial settings where both parties know they have not reached a binding agreement: in Cobbe v Yeoman's Row [2008] the developer's claim failed. Once an equity is established, the court decides how to satisfy it. In Guest v Guest [2022] the Supreme Court held that the aim is to remedy the unconscionability of the promisor's repudiation, and the starting point will usually be to fulfil the promise, unless that would be out of all proportion to the claimant's detriment, adjusted to avoid over-compensation (for example, by discounting for receiving the land early). In registered land, s116 of the 2002 Act confirms that the equity can bind successors from the time it arises.

questions.q: Raj is sole registered proprietor of a house. His partner Sue has a beneficial interest and lives there. Raj mortgages the house to a bank without telling Sue; the bank makes no enquiries of her. Is the bank bound by Sue's interest?
options: Yes, but only if the bank had actual knowledge of her interest
No, because interests under a trust can only be protected by a notice on the register
No, because the mortgage money overreached her interest
Yes, because she was in actual occupation, so her interest overrides under Schedule 3 para 2
questions.why: As in Boland, Sue's beneficial interest combined with obvious actual occupation overrides the registered charge, and she was not asked about it so the non-disclosure exception cannot apply. Interests under a trust cannot be protected by a notice at all (s33), so that cannot be the reason. Overreaching needs payment to at least two trustees, and Raj was the only one. Actual knowledge is relevant only if the occupation was not obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, which is not the case here.

questions.q: Tom buys a house with the help of a mortgage. Before completion, his mother, who contributed to the price and has been promised a share, moves some furniture in. Can her interest bind the lender?
options: Yes, because a contribution to the price always creates an overriding interest
No, because her interest is personal rather than proprietary
No: preparatory acts before completion are not actual occupation, and the purchase and mortgage are one transaction (Cann)
Yes, because she was in actual occupation once her furniture was in the house
questions.why: Cann held that moving furniture in before completion is preparatory and is not actual occupation, and that an acquisition mortgage takes effect at the same moment as the purchase, so there is no gap in which the mother's interest could gain priority. Treating furniture moved in early as occupation is the argument Cann rejected. A contribution may create a beneficial interest, but that interest overrides only with actual occupation at the relevant time. A beneficial interest under a trust is proprietary, so calling it personal is wrong.

questions.q: Explain the limits on the overriding interest of a person in actual occupation under Schedule 3, paragraph 2 of the Land Registration Act 2002.
markScheme: Interest must be proprietary and the person in actual occupation at the time of disposition (Cann: completion)
Only as to land actually occupied
Exception: failure to disclose on reasonable enquiry when it would have been reasonable to do so
Exception: occupation not obvious on reasonably careful inspection and buyer had no actual knowledge
Overreaching defeats the claim regardless of occupation (Flegg)
questions.modelAnswer: Paragraph 2 allows the proprietary interest of a person in actual occupation to bind a registered disponee without being on the register, but the 2002 Act narrowed the equivalent rule from the 1925 Act. First, the claimant must have a proprietary interest and be in actual occupation at the time of the disposition; in Abbey National v Cann [1991] this meant completion, and preparatory acts did not count. Secondly, the interest overrides only in relation to the land actually occupied. Thirdly, it does not override if the buyer made reasonable enquiry of the occupier and the occupier failed to disclose the interest when they could reasonably have been expected to. Fourthly, it does not override if the occupation would not have been obvious on a reasonably careful inspection and the buyer did not actually know of the interest. Finally, if the disposition overreaches the interest, as where capital money is paid to two trustees (City of London BS v Flegg [1988]), occupation will not help, because the interest is transferred to the proceeds.

questions.q: Sid has been in adverse possession of a registered plot for 11 years. He applies to be registered. The registered owner objects. No special circumstances apply. What happens?
options: The application fails, and Sid can never acquire title to registered land
Sid is registered, because 10 years' adverse possession is enough
Sid is registered, because the owner's title was extinguished after 12 years
The application fails; if Sid stays in adverse possession for two more years, he can reapply and will be registered
questions.why: Under Schedule 6 an objection defeats the first application unless a para 5 condition applies, and paras 6-7 give the squatter a second chance after two more years if not evicted. Ten years only entitles Sid to apply, so it does not guarantee registration against an objection. Extinguishment after 12 years is the unregistered land rule under the Limitation Act, which does not run against registered estates (s96). Saying title can never be acquired ignores the second application route.

questions.q: A farmer grazed a field under a licence that expired. The owner refused to renew it, but the farmer carried on grazing for 13 years and would have paid for a new licence if asked. The land is unregistered. Following Pye v Graham, which statement is correct?
options: The farmer had the intention to possess, and his willingness to pay does not prevent adverse possession
Adverse possession requires an intention to own the land, which the farmer lacked
Grazing can never amount to factual possession
The farmer's willingness to pay shows he lacked the intention to possess
questions.why: Pye held that the required intention is to possess, and that a squatter's readiness to pay for a licence if asked is consistent with that intention. The House of Lords rejected the argument that willingness to pay negates the intention. The test is intention to possess, not intention to own. Grazing combined with control of the land can be factual possession, as in Pye itself.

questions.q: How did the Land Registration Act 2002 change the law on adverse possession of registered land, and why?
markScheme: Old law: 12 years under Limitation Act; LRA 1925 s75 trust for squatter
s96: limitation no longer runs against registered estates
Sch 6: application after 10 years; notice and objection
Para 5 conditions: estoppel, some other right, boundary
Paras 6-7: second application after two further years
Reasons: register's conclusiveness; registered owner can be traced; fairness after Pye
questions.modelAnswer:
Before the 2002 Act, adverse possession of registered land worked like unregistered land: after 12 years the owner's right to recover was barred, and under s75 of the Land Registration Act 1925 the proprietor held the title on trust for the squatter. The 2002 Act changed this. Under s96 limitation no longer runs against a registered estate. Instead, under Schedule 6, a squatter who has been in adverse possession for 10 years may apply to be registered. The registered proprietor and others with interests are notified and can object. If they do, the application fails unless the squatter meets one of three conditions in para 5: estoppel, some other right to the land, or the boundary condition, which requires adjacent land, an unfixed boundary and a reasonable belief for 10 years that the land was the squatter's. If the application fails and the owner does not evict the squatter within two years, the squatter can reapply and will be registered (paras 6-7).

The reasons were that, with a registered title, the owner can always be identified and notified, so the traditional justification of preventing stale claims and lost title deeds is weaker. The reforms protect the register's reliability and prevent owners losing land through mere inactivity, as in Pye, while still allowing adverse possession where it is fair, as in boundary mistakes.

questions.q: Amy and Bea hold a house as legal and beneficial joint tenants. Amy posts a written notice of severance to Bea's home address. Before Bea sees it, Amy changes her mind, retrieves the letter from the doormat and destroys it. Has the joint tenancy been severed?
options: No, because severance requires the agreement of both joint tenants
Only the legal joint tenancy is severed
Yes, because a notice delivered to the co-owner's address is served even if not read (Kinch v Bullard)
No, because Bea never read the notice
questions.why: Kinch v Bullard held that a s36(2) notice is served once delivered to the recipient's address, so later destruction does not undo it. Actual reading is not required for service. A written notice is a unilateral method, so Bea's agreement is unnecessary. The legal estate can never be severed; only the beneficial joint tenancy can, so the claim about the legal joint tenancy is wrong.

questions.q: A bank wants an order for sale of a house co-owned by a mortgagor (who has defaulted) and her husband, who are not bankrupt. Which statement best reflects the law?
options: The court must refuse sale if children live in the house
The bank's interest is paramount, so sale will be ordered unless there are exceptional circumstances
The court weighs the s15 TOLATA factors, including the creditor's interests, but no single factor is automatically decisive
The court cannot order sale on a creditor's application, because only trustees may apply under s14
questions.why: Mortgage Corporation v Shaire held that s15 TOLATA requires a genuine balancing of factors, although Bell shows the creditor's interests often weigh heavily. The 'exceptional circumstances' test comes from bankruptcy cases under s335A Insolvency Act 1986, which do not apply here. Section 14 allows any person with an interest in the property, including a secured creditor, to apply. The welfare of minors is one factor, not an automatic bar.

questions.q: What is overreaching, and why did it protect the lender in City of London Building Society v Flegg but not in Williams & Glyn's Bank v Boland?
markScheme: Definition: beneficial interests detach from land and attach to proceeds
Requirement: capital money paid to at least two trustees or a trust corporation (LPA ss2, 27)
Flegg: two trustees received mortgage money, so interests overreached despite actual occupation
Boland: single trustee (husband), so no overreaching; wife's interest overrode
Comment on policy: protects purchasers; criticism that occupiers lose out
questions.modelAnswer: Overreaching is the process by which beneficial interests under a trust of land are detached from the land and attached to the money paid by a purchaser or lender, so the purchaser takes free of them. Under ss2 and 27 of the LPA 1925 it requires the capital money to be paid to at least two trustees or a trust corporation. In City of London BS v Flegg [1988] the Fleggs contributed to a house registered in the names of their daughter and son-in-law, and lived there. When the two registered owners mortgaged it, the money was paid to two trustees, so the Fleggs' interests were overreached and the lender took free of them, even though the Fleggs were in actual occupation. In Williams & Glyn's Bank v Boland [1981] the husband was the sole registered owner, so the mortgage money was paid to only one trustee and no overreaching took place. Mrs Boland's beneficial interest therefore remained attached to the land and, because she was in actual occupation, it bound the bank. Overreaching protects buyers and keeps trusts off the register, but critics argue it leaves occupiers like the Fleggs with only a claim against the trustees.

questions.q: Gina and Hal buy a house in joint names but make no declaration of trust. Gina pays 70% of the price. They later separate. What is the starting point under Stack v Dowden?
options: Gina owns 70% and Hal 30% under a resulting trust
The court divides the property in whatever way is fair, without needing to consider intention
Hal has no beneficial interest unless he made direct contributions
Equity follows the law, so they are presumed to be equal beneficial joint tenants; Gina must prove a different common intention
questions.why: Stack held that, in a domestic joint names case, beneficial joint tenancy is the starting point and the party claiming more must prove a different common intention from the whole course of dealing. The resulting trust presumption based purely on contributions was rejected for this context. Imputing fair shares is only possible once a common intention to depart from equality is shown and the shares cannot otherwise be inferred (Kernott). The direct-contribution focus comes from Rosset, which concerns sole name cases.

questions.q: Ian is the sole legal owner of a house. His partner Jo has paid household bills but never discussed ownership with him and made no contribution to the purchase. Following Geary v Rankine, what must Jo show first?
options: That they are joint tenants in equity, as equity follows the law
An actual common intention, express or inferred from conduct, that she should have a beneficial interest
Nothing: the court can impute a share to her if fair
That she contributed towards household expenses, which automatically gives her a proportionate share
questions.why: Geary v Rankine confirms that in a sole name case the existence of a common intention to share must be actual, whether expressed or inferred, and cannot be imputed; Rosset makes this hard without discussions or direct contributions. Imputation is only allowed at the quantification stage. Paying bills does not automatically create a share. 'Equity follows the law' would point to Ian as sole beneficial owner, since only he holds the legal title.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the approach to joint names and sole name cases after Stack v Dowden and Jones v Kernott.
markScheme: Joint names: presumption of beneficial joint tenancy (equity follows the law); burden on party asserting otherwise
Displacement by actual common intention, initial or later; imputation of fair shares if needed (Kernott)
Sole name: claimant must first establish common intention to share (Rosset) plus detrimental reliance
Acquisition cannot be imputed (Geary v Rankine); quantification looks at whole course of dealing (Abbott)
Evaluation: uncertainty, cost of litigation, Law Commission reform proposals
questions.modelAnswer:
In joint names cases the starting point is that equity follows the law, so the parties are presumed to be beneficial joint tenants with equal shares (Stack v Dowden [2007]). The burden is on the party claiming unequal shares to prove a different common intention, which may be found from the whole course of dealing in relation to the property and may have arisen at purchase or later. In Jones v Kernott [2011] the Supreme Court added that if it is clear the parties intended their shares to change but impossible to infer the actual shares, the court may impute an intention and award what is fair; Ms Jones was awarded 90%.

In sole name cases, the claimant has two hurdles. First, she must show a common intention that she should have a beneficial interest, with detrimental reliance. Lord Bridge in Lloyds Bank v Rosset [1991] required express discussions or direct contributions to the purchase price. This intention must be actual, not imputed (Geary v Rankine [2012]). Secondly, if she succeeds, her share is quantified by looking at the whole course of dealing, where the court can impute a fair share (Abbott v Abbott [2007]). The result is a more flexible approach to quantification but a high threshold for acquisition in sole name cases, which critics say produces uncertainty and expensive litigation; the Law Commission's 2007 proposals for cohabitants have not been implemented.

questions.q: Owen lets a bedsit to Pia at a weekly rent. The agreement is headed 'licence' and says Owen may enter at any time, but he never does and Pia has the only key. What is Pia most likely to have?
options: A tenancy, because she has exclusive possession for a term at a rent and the entry clause is a pretence
A licence, because rent alone cannot create a tenancy
A licence, because the parties labelled it a licence
A tenancy, but only if the agreement was made by deed
questions.why: Street v Mountford looks at substance: exclusive possession for a term (here periodic) at a rent creates a tenancy, and Antoniades shows that a clause never intended to be used is disregarded as a pretence. The label is not decisive, which is the point of the 'fork and spade' remark. Saying rent alone cannot create a tenancy misses the point: the tenancy rests on exclusive possession for a term, and here that is present alongside the rent. A weekly periodic tenancy at a market rent falls within s54(2) and needs no deed.

questions.q: A lease is granted to Acme Ltd, a company, 'until the landlord needs the land for development'. Rent is paid monthly. What is the most likely result?
options: The stated term is void for uncertainty, but a monthly periodic tenancy arises from the payment and acceptance of rent
A valid fixed-term lease ending when development begins
No tenancy of any kind, because the term is uncertain
A 90-year lease under s149(6) LPA 1925, as in Berrisford v Mexfield
questions.why: As in Prudential Assurance, the term is uncertain (Lace v Chantler), but the payment and acceptance of periodic rent gives rise to a periodic tenancy. A lease must have a certain maximum duration, so a fixed term ending on an uncertain event is invalid. Saying no tenancy exists ignores the implied periodic tenancy. Mexfield worked because, before 1926, an uncertain-term grant to an individual would have taken effect as a tenancy for the tenant's own life, which s149(6) converts into a 90-year term; a company has no life, so that route is not open to Acme Ltd.

questions.q: Explain how the courts distinguish leases from licences.
markScheme: Lease requires exclusive possession and term certain; rent not essential
Street v Mountford: substance over label; exceptions
Sham/pretence clauses (Antoniades v Villiers) and multiple occupiers (AG Securities v Vaughan)
Consequences: lease is proprietary and statutory protection; licence personal
Bruton: non-proprietary lease
