questions.modelAnswer: The key test comes from Street v Mountford [1985]: where a person is granted exclusive possession of premises for a term at a rent, there is a tenancy, whatever the parties call the arrangement. The court looks at the substance of the rights granted, not the label. There are exceptions where exclusive possession does not create a tenancy, such as a service occupancy, an act of friendship or generosity, or where there is no intention to create legal relations. Rent is not essential to a lease (Ashburn Anstalt), but a term certain is. The courts disregard terms that are pretences: in Antoniades v Villiers [1990] a clause allowing the owner to move strangers into a small flat shared by a couple was never intended to be used, so they were joint tenants. But in AG Securities v Vaughan, occupiers who arrived at different times on separate agreements lacked the four unities and joint exclusive possession, so they were licensees. The distinction matters because a lease is an estate in land that can bind third parties and attracts statutory protection, whereas a licence is personal. Bruton [2000] shows that even a grantor with no estate can create a contractual tenancy between the parties.

questions.q: The owner of a holiday village grants neighbouring holiday flats the right to use the village's swimming pool and golf course. Following Regency Villas [2018], can this be an easement?
options: No, because purely recreational rights can never be easements
No, because any right requiring the servient owner to spend money is invalid
Yes, but only if the servient owner also covenants to maintain the facilities
Yes, because recreational rights can accommodate dominant land used for leisure
questions.why: The Supreme Court held that recreational and sporting rights can be easements where they accommodate dominant land used for leisure, as with the timeshare flats. The idea that recreation can never qualify was rejected. The rule that an easement cannot require the servient owner to spend money did not defeat these rights, because they required only passivity: the servient owner was under no duty to run or maintain the facilities. For the same reason no maintenance covenant is required.

questions.q: Vic owns two adjoining houses and lives in one. For years he has used a drive over the second house to reach his garage. He sells the second house and keeps the first, without expressly reserving a right of way. Which statement is correct?
options: Vic will struggle: Wheeldon v Burrows and s62 operate in favour of the buyer, so he must rely on necessity or common intention, which are narrow
Vic automatically has a right of way by prescription because he used the drive for years
Vic has an easement under s62 LPA because he used the drive before the sale
Vic has an easement under Wheeldon v Burrows, which operates in favour of the seller
questions.why: Wheeldon v Burrows and s62 benefit the grantee (the buyer of the part sold); a seller who wants rights over the land he sells must normally reserve them expressly, and implied reservation is limited to necessity or common intention. Saying Wheeldon v Burrows works for the seller reverses the rule. Prescription cannot run while one person owns both plots, because a person cannot have an easement over his own land. Section 62 passes rights with the land conveyed, which here is the second house, not Vic's retained house.

questions.q: Explain how easements may be implied on the sale of part of a plot of land.
markScheme: Necessity (land otherwise inaccessible; Nickerson v Barraclough)
Common intention (Wong v Beaumont)
Wheeldon v Burrows: continuous and apparent, necessary for reasonable enjoyment, in use at time of grant
s62 LPA: converts advantages into easements; diversity of occupation or continuous and apparent (Wood v Waddington)
Grant v reservation asymmetry
questions.modelAnswer: When an owner sells part of his land, the buyer may acquire easements over the retained land without express words. First, necessity: if the part sold would be landlocked, a right of access is implied, based on the parties' presumed intention (Nickerson v Barraclough [1981]). Secondly, common intention: where both parties intend the land to be used for a particular purpose, easements needed for that use are implied, as with the ventilation duct in Wong v Beaumont Property Trust [1965]. Thirdly, under Wheeldon v Burrows (1879) quasi-easements used by the common owner pass to the buyer if they are continuous and apparent, necessary for the reasonable enjoyment of the land sold, and in use at the time of the sale. Fourthly, s62 LPA 1925 passes all rights and advantages appertaining to the land, which can upgrade a licence into an easement (Wright v Macadam [1949]); prior diversity of occupation is traditionally required but not where the right is continuous and apparent (Wood v Waddington [2015]). These rules favour buyers: a seller who wants rights over the part sold must normally reserve them expressly, since implied reservation is limited to necessity and common intention.

questions.q: In 2015 Kay sold part of her land to Lee, who covenanted (in a registered transfer) 'not to build more than one house' and 'to maintain the boundary fence'. The covenants were noted on Lee's title. Lee has sold to Max. Which covenants bind Max?
options: Both, because both were noted on the register
Neither, because covenants never bind successors of freehold land
Only the fence covenant, because positive covenants run with the land in equity
Only the building covenant, because the burden of a positive covenant does not run (Rhone v Stephens)
questions.why: The building restriction is negative in substance and can bind Max under Tulk v Moxhay if registered, but the fence covenant is positive and its burden does not run at law or in equity (Austerberry; Rhone v Stephens). Noting on the register protects only interests capable of binding, so it cannot make a positive covenant run. Restrictive covenants do bind successors in equity, so 'never' is wrong. The fence option reverses the rule.

questions.q: A covenant states that the purchaser will not use the land 'except as a single private dwelling'. How is this classified?
options: Restrictive, because in substance it prevents other uses and requires no expenditure
Neither, because covenants about use cannot bind land
Positive, because the words 'single private dwelling' impose an obligation
Positive, because the covenantor must use the land as a dwelling
questions.why: The test is substance: this covenant limits how the land can be used and does not require the owner to act or spend money, so it is negative and can run under Tulk v Moxhay. The covenantor is not forced to use the land at all, so calling it positive confuses wording with substance. Restrictive covenants about use are the classic type that can bind successors. Framing in terms of a permitted use does not make the covenant positive.

questions.q: How can the benefit of a restrictive covenant pass to a successor in title of the covenantee in equity?
markScheme: Annexation: express words or statutory annexation under s78 (Federated Homes)
Land must be identifiable (Crest Nicholson); annexation to each and every part
Assignment: express assignment with transfer of land
Building schemes (Elliston v Reacher)
Covenant must touch and concern the land
questions.modelAnswer: In equity the benefit of a restrictive covenant can pass in three ways, provided the covenant touches and concerns the land. First, by annexation, which attaches the benefit permanently to the covenantee's land. This can be done expressly, or by statute: in Federated Homes v Mill Lodge Properties [1980] the Court of Appeal held that s78 LPA 1925 automatically annexes the benefit of a covenant relating to the covenantee's land to each and every part of it. Crest Nicholson v McAllister [2004] added that the benefited land must be identifiable from the covenant document. Secondly, by express assignment, where the benefit is assigned to the purchaser at the same time as the land. Thirdly, by a building scheme, where a developer lays out an estate in plots subject to common covenants intended to be mutually enforceable by all purchasers, as set out in Elliston v Reacher [1908]. Once the benefit has passed, the successor can enforce the covenant against anyone bound by the burden.

questions.q: A wife charges her share of the family home to secure her husband's business overdraft. The bank sends documents via the husband and takes no other steps. She later proves he unduly influenced her. Can the bank enforce the charge against her?
options: Yes, because a joint loan never puts a lender on inquiry
No, because the bank was put on inquiry and did not take the Etridge steps, so it has constructive notice of the undue influence
No, because any charge given by a wife over the family home is void
Yes, because a lender is never responsible for undue influence by a third party
questions.why: Under Etridge a lender is put on inquiry whenever the surety's relationship with the debtor is non-commercial, and failing to take the steps (direct contact, independent solicitor's confirmation) leaves it fixed with notice. The 'never responsible' claim ignores the notice doctrine in O'Brien and Etridge. Pitt concerned a joint loan for joint purposes, whereas this is a surety transaction for the husband's debts. Such charges are valid if the lender follows the Etridge steps.

questions.q: A lender sells a repossessed house quickly at auction during a slow market, below what it might have fetched six months later. The sale was properly advertised and it obtained the best price available at the time. Has the lender breached its duty?
options: Yes, because it must wait for the best possible market
Yes, because a lender must obtain the borrower's consent to the timing of sale
No, because a lender owes the borrower no duties when selling
No, because the lender can choose when to sell, provided it takes reasonable care to obtain the true market value at that time
questions.why: Cuckmere Brick requires reasonable care to get the true market value at the time of sale, and Silven confirms the lender can choose the timing. The idea that the lender must wait for a better market was rejected in Silven and China and South Sea Bank v Tan. No consent to timing is required. The lender does owe duties of good faith and reasonable care as to price, so saying it owes none is wrong.

questions.q: What is a 'clog on the equity of redemption'? Illustrate with cases.
markScheme: Equity of redemption: right to redeem on payment; 'once a mortgage always a mortgage'
Options to purchase in the mortgage void (Samuel v Jarrah Timber); separate later option may be valid (Reeve v Lisle)
Postponement: valid if not illusory and commercial (Knightsbridge v Byrne); illusory void (Fairclough v Swan Brewery)
Collateral advantages: valid unless unfair/unconscionable or clog (Kreglinger)
Comment on commercial v consumer contexts
questions.modelAnswer: The equity of redemption is the borrower's right to recover the mortgaged property free of the mortgage once the debt is repaid. Equity treats a mortgage as security only, so it strikes down terms, known as clogs, that prevent or restrict redemption: "once a mortgage, always a mortgage". An option for the lender to purchase the property granted as part of the mortgage is void, because it could stop the borrower recovering the land (Samuel v Jarrah Timber [1904]), but an option granted in a separate, independent transaction later on can be valid (Reeve v Lisle [1902]). Postponing the date of redemption is not in itself a clog: in Knightsbridge Estates v Byrne [1939] a 40-year postponement between commercial parties was upheld. However, a postponement that makes redemption illusory is void, as in Fairclough v Swan Brewery [1912], where a mortgage of a lease could only be redeemed weeks before the lease ended. Collateral advantages for the lender, such as a trading arrangement, can survive redemption if they are not unfair or unconscionable and do not clog redemption (Kreglinger [1914]). The courts are more willing to uphold terms between commercial parties of equal bargaining strength.

questions.q: Problem question. Ali is the sole registered proprietor of a house. His partner Bea paid £30,000 towards the purchase price, and they agreed when buying it that it would be 'our home'. Bea lives there, but in March she went to care for her mother in Spain for three months, leaving her furniture and belongings in the house. While she was away, Ali mortgaged the house to Credit Bank, which did not inspect or make any enquiries. Ali's lodger, Dev, occupies the attic under an oral two-year tenancy at a market rent. Ali's neighbour, Ned, has walked across Ali's garden to reach the road every day for 25 years without asking permission. Ali has now defaulted on the loan, and Credit Bank wants possession and sale of the house free of everyone's rights. Advise Bea, Dev and Ned.
markScheme: Bea's beneficial interest: sole name constructive trust (Rosset, express agreement plus direct contribution; Stack/Abbott quantification) or resulting trust

Priority: s29 LRA 2002; interest not on register; Sch 3 para 2 actual occupation despite temporary absence (Link Lending; Chhokar-type reasoning); obvious on inspection/no enquiry so exceptions not met
No overreaching: single trustee (Boland v Flegg); bank bound
Effect: bank can still seek sale under s14 TOLATA; s15 factors; Shaire and Bell
Dev: legal periodic/2-year lease within s54(2), no deed needed; overrides under Sch 3 para 1 (and para 2); lease vs licence (Street v Mountford)
Ned: prescriptive easement (20 years as of right, nec vi nec clam nec precario); legal; overrides under Sch 3 para 3 (exercised within the year / obvious)
Possession: s36 AJA 1970 protections for Ali; reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Bea. As Bea is not on the title, she needs a beneficial interest under a constructive trust. In a sole name case she must show an actual common intention that she should have a share, plus detrimental reliance (Lloyds Bank v Rosset). The agreement that it would be "our home" and her direct contribution of £30,000 satisfy even Lord Bridge's strict test. Her share is quantified from the whole course of dealing (Stack v Dowden; Abbott v Abbott).

The registered charge takes priority over interests not protected at registration (s29 LRA 2002). A trust interest cannot be protected by notice (s33), so Bea must rely on Schedule 3 para 2. Temporary absence does not necessarily end actual occupation: in Link Lending v Bustard a woman in a care home remained in occupation because of her belongings, visits and intention to return. Bea's furniture and her intention to return after three months point the same way. The exceptions do not apply: no enquiry was made of her, and her occupation would have been obvious on a reasonably careful inspection, judged objectively. Overreaching is impossible because the money was paid to one trustee (Boland, contrasting Flegg). Her interest therefore probably binds the bank.

However, the bank can apply for sale under s14 TOLATA. The court weighs the s15 factors, including the purpose of providing a home and the bank's interests as secured creditor. These are not paramount (Mortgage Corporation v Shaire), but in Bank of Ireland v Bell sale was ordered where the debt was large and growing. Sale is likely, with Bea's share paid to her ahead of the bank.

Dev. An oral two-year tenancy at a market rent taking effect in possession is a legal lease under s54(2) LPA 1925, if Dev has exclusive possession of the attic (Street v Mountford). If Ali provides services and keeps control, Dev may be a mere licensee whose personal right cannot bind the bank. If he is a tenant, his lease of seven years or less overrides under Schedule 3 para 1, and it predates the charge.

Ned. Daily use for 25 years without force, secrecy or permission is use as of right, so Ned has probably acquired a legal easement by prescription (lost modern grant or the Prescription Act 1832). Although unregistered, it overrides under Schedule 3 para 3 because it was exercised within the year before the charge and is likely obvious on inspection.

Possession. Ali may ask the court to adjourn possession under s36 Administration of Justice Act 1970 if he can clear the arrears within a reasonable period (Norgan). Otherwise the bank will obtain possession and sale, subject to Dev's lease and Ned's easement, and with Bea's interest either binding the bank or satisfied from the proceeds of a TOLATA sale.

questions.q: Essay. 'The Land Registration Act 2002 set out to make the register a complete and accurate record of title. Overriding interests and adverse possession show that it has only partly succeeded.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains aims of LRA 2002 (Law Com No 271): register as complete and accurate as possible; mirror principle; e-conveyancing ambitions
Overriding interests reduced: Sch 3 narrower than LRA 1925 s70(1)(g); leases cut to 7 years; easements limited (para 3)
Actual occupation retained: justification (protects occupiers who would not think to register; Boland) versus cost to purchasers
Case law on actual occupation and exceptions (Cann, Link Lending), and overreaching as a counterweight (Flegg)
Adverse possession: Sch 6 regime, 10 years, notice and objection, para 5 conditions; s96
Assessment of the adverse possession reforms (Pye, ECtHR), boundary condition, residual risk
Other limits on completeness: alteration/rectification and indemnity (Sch 4, Sch 8); fraud
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The Land Registration Act 2002 followed the Law Commission's report Land Registration for the Twenty-First Century (Law Com No 271, 2001), which aimed to make the register as complete and accurate a record of title as possible, so that title could be checked with minimal further enquiry. Overriding interests and adverse possession are the main departures from that aim.

Overriding interests. The 2002 Act narrowed the categories that existed under the 1925 Act. Legal leases override only if seven years or less (Schedule 3 para 1), instead of 21 years. Legal easements override only if known, obvious on a reasonably careful inspection or recently exercised (para 3), and equitable easements no longer override. Actual occupation survives in para 2, but only for land actually occupied, and not where the occupier failed to disclose the interest on reasonable enquiry, or where occupation was not obvious and the buyer did not know of it.

Keeping actual occupation is a deliberate choice. People like Mrs Boland acquire interests informally and would not think to register them, and it would be harsh to deprive them of their homes. The cost is that buyers and lenders must inspect and ask questions, so the register is not a complete mirror; Link Lending v Bustard shows that "occupation" can exist without physical presence. Yet the law protects purchasers in other ways: overreaching (Flegg), the timing rule in Abbey National v Cann and the para 2 exceptions all place risk on silent occupiers.

Adverse possession. The Act transformed adverse possession of registered land. Limitation no longer runs (s96). A squatter with 10 years' possession may apply, the owner is notified, and an objection defeats the application unless a para 5 condition applies, although the squatter can reapply after two more years if not evicted. Owners are therefore unlikely to lose land through inaction as Pye did, and title rests on registration rather than possession. Adverse possession still matters in boundary disputes under para 5(4), because the register does not fix exact boundaries, and in unregistered land.

Other limits. Fraud and mistake also make the register inaccurate. Schedule 4 permits alteration and rectification, and Schedule 8 provides an indemnity (Swift 1st v Chief Land Registrar). This insurance principle accepts that perfect accuracy is impossible and compensates instead.

Conclusion. The Act has largely succeeded: overriding interests are narrower and squatters rarely defeat registered owners. Its success is partial only because Parliament chose to protect occupiers and boundary claimants where strict reliance on the register would cause injustice. A completely conclusive register was never a realistic or desirable goal.
